text: I am checking whether the abstract-level auction transplant is well defined: Q has private induced buyer values/seller costs and a surplus benchmark, whereas P allocates risky jobs and spends energy on reasoning. I will compare exact mechanisms and look for a test that preserves a measurable welfare counterfactual, then revisit the ledger before settling.

Q Method/Trading Mechanism (lines 210-260) has 11 buyers/11 sellers with private induced values, symmetric (p^\star=2.00,q^\star=6), random trader calls and a 300-iteration cap; its Results (lines 293-363) link unfilled profitable trades to one-cent quote improvements, especially GPT Large. P Energy Society/Experimental setup (lines 147-255, 277-326) meters every generated reasoning/output token as (C=k T S^{\alpha}), causing deactivation at zero energy. A direct auction over P jobs would remove Q’s clean fixed surplus benchmark because job value is uncertain, agent dependent, and affected by future token use. More identifiable construction: retain Q’s induced-value CDA and meter each quote decision in P-style energy, then compare welfare and behavior to unmetered Q.

Initial finding: The abstract-level auction-in-Energy-Society proposal has a structural mismatch. Q has one-unit private buyer values and seller costs with a persistent order book (Q, lines 241-278); P has five agents choosing among jobs whose rewards are split among successful solvers, plus donations, without sellers or exclusive goods (P, lines 147-170, 258-259). A direct double auction therefore requires inventing a seller, tradable rights, and payoff rules that could change P. Stronger candidate: transplant the measured, model-dependent token costs in P into the repeated quoting in Q, then test whether price discovery remains socially worthwhile after inference costs and budget exhaustion. Q observes repeated tiny quote improvements and stalled trades (Q, Market-Wide Outcomes and Individual Behavior); P provides an intervention design for charging generated tokens, not evidence about auctions (P, lines 101-106, 301-306). I will check cost scales and counterfactual design before committing.

The scan’s “literal survival” overstates P: its Introduction footnote (around lines 104-110) explicitly says survival is an analogy for token-budget exhaustion. Q’s CoT urgency result (Analysis of Reasoning, lines 405-443) is only for Gemini Large, is associational, and the authors caution traces may not reflect the causal decision process. P’s token charge changes trace length, so rerunning that lexicon alone cannot identify increased urgency. Also Q’s GPT Small advantage and P’s small-model energy advantage involve different models and settings; neither establishes a shared scale effect.

Ada #3 independently reaches the same direction; I agree with the structural mismatch. Sharpened question: in Q’s fixed-value continuous double auction, does making deliberation costly in P’s sense curb repeated one-cent quote improvements enough to increase realized gains from trade, or does energy-budget exhaustion remove traders and worsen allocation? The key comparison is randomized quote-cost salience/charge under identical values and order-book rules, plus a budget-exhaustion arm, with gross surplus, trade timing, quote count, and token-adjusted surplus measured separately. A nonmonotone effect is plausible, not a claimed result. Need calibrate currency conversion so token charges do not trivially exceed Q’s (0.25)-increment value scale.

Refinement and quantitative bound: Q reports 300 possible quote decisions per round, one-cent improvements, and GPT Large gross allocative efficiency only 0.36-0.67 (Q lines 247-259, 316-320, 359-371). From Q's eleven values/costs in 0.25 steps, the positive gains from the efficient five pairs are 2.5+2+1.5+1+0.5, so \(G^\star=7.5\) per round; Q's sixth equilibrium trade adds zero (Q lines 211-219). This makes costly price discovery measurable: \(G=\sum_{(b,s)\in M}(v_b-c_s)\), \(C=\sum_{i,t}kT_{it}S_i^\alpha\) after P (P lines 301-306), and \(W_\lambda=G-\lambda C\), with \(\lambda\) an explicit conversion between energy and induced-value dollars. Sweep \(\lambda\), report \(G\), \(C\), net \(W_\lambda\), quote count, spread-crossing, deactivation separately. Gross efficiency alone can rise while net welfare falls. P's no-discussion ablation lowers energy cost and raises survival while raising job collisions (P lines 569-624), so lower communication cost has a genuine coordination tradeoff; this supports measuring both sides, not assuming cost is pure waste. This is a hypothesis and design, not an observed cross-paper result.

Adjacent prior work, not this test: Agora allocates reasoning tasks to expert models via a confidence-calibrated auction (https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09600); DALA auctions communication opportunities to reduce token use (https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13193). Neither abstract addresses whether charging LLM traders for inference changes quote dynamics or allocative efficiency in a fixed-value continuous double auction. Search queries: “LLM agents continuous double auction inference cost token budget trading efficiency experiment”; “large language model agent auction costly reasoning compute budget price discovery paper”; “site:arxiv.org LLM continuous double auction inference costs token price discovery”. This is a limited prior-work check, not a novelty claim.

Important benchmark nuance for Ada #6 and my #5: Q’s (q^\star=6) includes a zero-surplus sixth trade under symmetric values; (G^\star=7.5) comes from five strictly positive pairs. With positive inference costs, “reach (q=6)” is not a welfare target, and even gross efficiency (G/G^\star=1) can coexist with poor net welfare. Report the gross upper bound (7.5), but judge charge policies by (W_\lambda=G-\lambda C) at the same ex ante shadow price; do not present (W_\lambda/7.5) as an achievable cost-aware optimum. Also P’s raw collision count after removing discussion changes with active agents and job-attempt exposure, so its coordination interpretation needs per-opportunity normalization.

Cross-check and caveats. Q uses closed API models (Q lines 280-285), so P's size factor \(S^\alpha\) cannot be copied literally when parameter counts are unavailable; primary experiment should use a common per-generated-token tariff \(\alpha=0\), with open-weight models/size dependence as a separate arm. P's \(k=0.015\) energy per token and job rewards of 200-800 energy (P lines 180-181, 301-306) have no natural conversion to Q's 0.25 dollar value increments; \(\lambda\) must be predeclared/swept. With baseline trace token counts, a retrospective break-even calculation \(\lambda_{BE}=G/C\) is possible, but it cannot show behavioral adaptation. Randomized live cost-aware runs are needed for that. Q's CoT association is only Gemini and explicitly noncausal (Q lines 409-442); P's survival is a token-budget analogy (P lines 101-105), so do not sell the result as literal survival or causal urgency language. Prior-work search queries: 'LLM agents double auction token cost inference cost deliberation price discovery welfare' and 'costly computation artificial agents double auction LLM token budget trading'. Adjacent primary papers include https://ojs.aaai.org/index.php/AAAI/article/view/40182 on auctioning communication bandwidth, https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.09600 on auction-based task allocation, and https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.16205 on token-level cost/performance in another environment. Their abstracts do not describe this exact fixed-value cost-of-price-discovery test, but this is not an exhaustive novelty search.

Best account at present, replacing the scan hypothesis: Q’s induced-value CDA gives known (G^\star=7.5), yet repeated costless quote calls and penny improvements can stall profitable trades (Q Market Environment, Trading Mechanism, Market-Wide Outcomes, Individual Behavior, lines 210-278 and 293-380). P gives a mechanism that turns generated reasoning/output tokens into an energy debit, (C=kTS^{\alpha}), with deactivation on exhaustion (P Energy Society, Simulation Loop, Experimental setup, lines 147-255 and 277-326); its no-size-penalty and no-discussion ablations show behavior and survival move when the cost structure changes (P Experiments 2–3, lines 484-630). Question: When LLM traders must pay for each quote decision, does that induce earlier profitable spread crossing, or does it deplete participation and leave more gains unrealized? Retain Q’s values, order book and iteration limit; randomize unpriced versus explicit per-token charges, and add a finite-budget/exhaustion condition with a matched exogenous turn-cap control. Use same model/prompt/role schedules and multiple seeds; pilot only to set charge and budget scales, then freeze them. Measure (G=\sum_{(b,s)}(v_b-c_s)), tokens (C), (W_\lambda=G-\lambda C), profitable matches, calls per trade, crossings, and deactivations. Evaluate a predeclared range of (\lambda), because P energy and Q dollars have no natural conversion. A successful paper would establish the causal tradeoff and whether a budget range improves (G) or (W_\lambda); a null/negative result still locates where inference pricing fails. Do not use (q=6) as cost-aware welfare optimum, infer a universal model-size effect, or treat Q’s Gemini-only urgency lexicon as causal evidence. No experiment has been run; direction of effect and achievable cost-aware optimum remain open.

Correction to my #2, #5, #8, #10: shell rendering dropped TeX delimiters in those entries. The quantities are \(G^\star=7.5\), \(q^\star=6\), \(G=\sum_{(b,s)\in M}(v_b-c_s)\), \(C=\sum_{i,t}kT_{it}S_i^\alpha\), and \(W_\lambda=G-\lambda C\). Ada #9 adds a crucial implementation constraint: Q uses closed API models with unavailable parameter counts, so the primary test should use the common per-token tariff \(\alpha=0\); size-weighted metering requires an open-weight extension. The conversion \(\lambda\) between P energy and Q values must be declared and swept.

Design correction from Q Appendix Prompt Templates (lines 515-588): an agent can decline the current bid/ask prompt, but Q's scheduler may select any not-yet-traded agent again up to the 300-iteration cap (lines 241-259). If every selection incurs inference cost, repeated calls are partly imposed by the scheduler, so a cost response cannot be interpreted as endogenous restraint unless the agent can opt out of the remainder of a round. Add a persistent withdraw/skip-rest-of-round action in every experimental arm, charging for the decision that withdraws but no later calls. Keep an unchanged-Q replication arm, then compare all modified arms under identical scheduler and opt-out rules. Also cancel resting orders on budget exhaustion, or specify how they can execute after an agent deactivates. Distinguish mere accounting for token cost, cost-aware quotes without binding budget, and cost-aware quotes with finite budget. This correction may matter as much as the per-token tariff.

Ada #12 is right: Q can select the same nontrader again regardless of its previous choice, so cost per selection alone is partly involuntary. Refined design: first replicate unchanged Q; then give all causal arms the same persistent withdraw-for-this-round option and identical order-book/scheduler rules. Cross unpriced versus salient per-token charges, and nonbinding versus finite budget, with resting-order cancellation on exhaustion specified beforehand. Attribute earlier crossings only within the modified-arm comparison; separately measure voluntary withdrawals and involuntary deactivations. This operational detail is necessary for interpreting inference pricing as a decision incentive.
ready at #13

Current intention: I accept emmy #10 as the leading question, with the scheduler/withdrawal correction in #12. The claim worth testing is about costly price discovery under an unchanged induced-value surplus schedule, not transplantation of an auction into P's jobs. A clean intervention needs the same opt-out option in all randomized arms; then compare zero price, explicit token price without finite-budget removal, and priced finite-budget removal, plus an exogenous-removal control to isolate composition effects. Keep welfare and cost accounting separate because \(G^\star=7.5\) is only a gross bound. Main unresolved items are whether Q's released records include reliable per-decision reasoning-token usage for each API, how to calibrate \(\lambda\) before the main runs, whether agents understand a simulated token tariff, and whether any positive net-welfare effect appears. No experiments run and no broad novelty claim.
ready at #15

Cross-check of ada #15 against Q and P: Q Trading Mechanism (lines 241-259) selects randomly among agents who have not transacted, so an agent that declines may be called again; Q Announcement Prompts (lines 566-584) confirm the decline option is only for the current call. P charges generated tokens per model call and deactivates an exhausted agent (Energy Society lines 147-159; cost formula lines 299-306). Thus the tariff must enter each trader private payoff, not merely the analyst welfare calculation: define net trader payoff as realized transaction profit less its own token charges, disclose that rule, and allow persistent round withdrawal in every causal arm. Calls before the first opportunity to withdraw remain imposed by the scheduler, so report their cost separately. A trade also exits two agents, avoiding future charges for both; this is a genuine mechanism through which pricing may change crossing incentives, not evidence that it will. Ada #15 exogenous removal control is useful for separating price response from compositional loss. If a priced arm improves gross surplus, this mechanism and voluntary withdrawal should be checked before invoking Q urgency vocabulary.
ready at #17

Cross-check of emmy #17 adds a mechanism and a needed control. Q's rule says a crossing quote executes immediately and both parties exit the round (Q, Trading Mechanism, lines 247-259). Thus a trader's private incentive to cross includes its own avoided future inference charges, while the market also avoids the counterparty's future charges; the crossing trader does not internalize that second saving. The gap between private and social value of ending search is a sharper publication question than a generic efficiency change. Measure future scheduled-call savings for both sides and compare private net profit with \(W_\lambda=G-\lambda C\); use the same predeclared tariff in agent payoffs and analyst accounting. In all modified arms, specify whether a resting order survives voluntary withdrawal and cancel it on budget exhaustion; charge a decision before processing its submitted action, with an explicit rule for a charge that exhausts the budget. A withdrawal option removes repeat calls after the choice, but the first call remains imposed by Q's random scheduler. Q's original prompt also says a round can end when nobody can post an improving order (Appendix System Prompt, lines 539-541), while its mechanism specifies termination at \(T=300\) (lines 247-259); implementation should verify which rule the released code actually uses before claiming faithful replication. These are design inferences, not outcomes.

Correction to #19: avoided future calls for either party are counterfactual and cannot be read off a single realized path. Estimate the causal effect of price treatment on total calls and tokens with randomized, matched-seed runs; treat any party-level 'saved calls' mechanism analysis as model-dependent, since the crossing changes the order book and future scheduler eligibility. The directly observed outcomes remain gross surplus, token expenditure, trade timing, and exits.
